Bitter End
BIT-er end
noun (Navy); in the phrase to the bitter end
Nautical. A bitt is a wooden or iron post set through a ship’s deck to make lines fast. The Naval History and Heritage Command (NHHC) explains that a turn of line around a bitt is called a bitter, so the last part of the line, secured to the bitts, is the bitter end. Sailors now use it for the end of any line, and landsmen took it up in “to the bitter end.”

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The bitter end is the inboard end of a line or anchor cable, the part made fast to the bitts on deck. When the cable has run out to the bitter end, there is nothing more to pay out. NHHC records that ashore the phrase became “stick to the bitter end” and “faithful to the bitter end,” used of anyone who keeps to a course whatever it costs. The word has nothing to do with bitterness; it comes from the bitts. The Christian observation: the Christian life is a line paid out to its last fathom. “He that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved” (Mat 24:13). We are partakers of Christ “if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end” (Heb 3:14). And the Lord’s word to the church at Smyrna is the bitter end made glorious: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

The inboard end of a line or cable, made fast to the bitts (NHHC); hence to the bitter end, to the very last. Faithfulness unto death (Rev 2:10).

expand to see more

BITTER END, n. (Navy) The end of a line or cable secured to the bitts; in general use, the end of any line. From bitt, a deck post, and bitter, a turn of line around it (Naval History and Heritage Command).

TO THE BITTER END, phr. To the very last, whatever the consequences.

Key Scripture

Mat 24:13 — "But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved."

Heb 3:14 — "For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;"

Rev 2:10 — "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

Modern Corruption

NHHC notes the shore phrase can describe holding a course “without regard to consequences”; stubbornness in a wrong course is not the perseverance Scripture praises.

expand to see more

“To the bitter end” can praise two very different men. One holds to the truth when it costs him everything. The other holds to his own plan because he will not admit he was wrong. The phrase sounds the same for both, and pride is glad of the cover.

Scripture’s perseverance is faithfulness to Christ, not loyalty to one’s own course. The saints endure because God keeps them, and they hold fast to the confidence they began with (Heb 3:14). A man who has run out his line in the wrong direction is called to repent, not to admire his own grit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

bitt (deck post) → bitter (a turn of line around it) → bitter end, the last of the line at the bitts → to the bitter end ashore (NHHC).

expand to see more

bitt: a wooden or iron post through a ship’s deck for securing lines

bitter: a turn of line around a bitt

Ashore: “stick to the bitter end,” “faithful to the bitter end” (NHHC)

Usage

"“Veer the cable, but not to the bitter end.”"

"But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. (Mat 24:13)."
